q1: Because the entity is still unconfirmed, I would favor a broadly active, CNS-penetrant, well-tolerated option over an entity-specific intensive regimen: single-agent oral temozolomide is a reasonable way to start, given its CNS penetration, oral route, and generally favorable toxicity profile, and it is active across several candidate entities (high-grade mesenchymal/spindle-cell neoplasms, several sarcoma subtypes, and gliomas). Other options worth naming, to be weighed once the entity is clearer, include a vincristine-based multi-agent combination if a small round-cell/rhabdomyosarcoma-type sarcoma remains in the differential, and an anthracycline-containing regimen, the standard sarcoma backbone; both carry more acute toxicity and are better reserved until the entity is better defined, with dose intensification or a second agent to be considered once I see how she tolerates a first agent. I would also check whether a clinical trial is open to her, since the entity remains unconfirmed. I would avoid committing to a single entity-specific 'gold standard' regimen as if the diagnosis were already established.
q2: Yes. Given the entity is still unconfirmed and the disease has been growing, escalating from single-agent temozolomide to temozolomide plus irinotecan (the TEMIRI combination) is a reasonable next step: this combination has real-world precedent in relapsed/refractory CNS tumors and in recurrent Ewing sarcoma, is usually well tolerated, and she has already demonstrated she tolerates temozolomide without significant toxicity. Adding irinotecan increases the chance of disease control while we continue working toward a definitive diagnosis. I would monitor more closely for the toxicities irinotecan adds, chiefly diarrhea and myelosuppression, and would dose-adjust or hold either drug if those become limiting.
q3: No, I would not stop chemotherapy and switch to FGFR-directed targeted therapy at this point; I would continue the current temozolomide-plus-irinotecan regimen. Reasons: (1) The entity itself is still not established (high-grade spindle cell/mesenchymal neoplasm, NOS, STAT6 negative) - an FGFR2 fusion is not a validated predictive biomarker for this specific, unconfirmed entity; its actionability is best established in cholangiocarcinoma, and evidence for FGFR-directed therapy in CNS/mesenchymal tumors is limited to case reports and small series, not a standard of care. (2) The co-occurring KRAS, STK11, and CTNNB1 alterations are not an established co-actionable signature with an FGFR2 fusion in this tumor type; this combination is atypical, and raises the possibility of a passenger alteration, a technical/low-variant-allele-fraction artifact of circulating tumor DNA, or genuinely complex tumor biology, rather than a clean single-driver story - it does not by itself strengthen the case for FGFR-directed monotherapy. (3) This is a plasma liquid-biopsy finding, not confirmed on tissue; a cell-free DNA result has a real false-positive and specificity risk, especially for disease that may be largely CNS-confined, and ideally would be correlated with tissue before making a major therapy change. (4) Available FGFR inhibitors (e.g. pemigatinib, erdafitinib, futibatinib, infigratinib) have blood-brain-barrier penetration limitations, which further weakens the case for switching away from a regimen she is tolerating and that may be controlling disease. My plan is to continue temozolomide plus irinotecan, pursue tissue correlation of the FGFR2 fusion if feasible, present the result at the molecular tumor board, and keep an FGFR inhibitor in reserve - via a clinical trial or compassionate-use pathway - if the disease progresses on chemotherapy or if further evidence supports its actionability, rather than switching to it now on this evidence alone.
